reasoning.Student A:
I prefer x > z > y > w. The matching will depend on submitted rankings and schools' priorities. Important points:

- If the mechanism is the standard student-proposing deferred-acceptance (DA) / strategy-proof school-choice algorithm, it is a dominant strategy for me to report my true preferences. So I should submit x > z > y > w regardless of others' rankings or my priority positions.
- My priorities: I have top priority (1) at y and w, and lower priority (2) at x and z. That means I am more likely to get y or w if many applicants apply there. However, most applicants prefer y first, so y will be highly contested—my high priority at y improves my chance, but it doesn’t change that truthful reporting is best under DA.
- The only plausible strategic deviation would be to list y above x or z to “lock in” a likely seat at y given my high priority. But that risks getting y when I could have gotten my more-preferred x or z if I had reported truthfully. Under a strategy-proof mechanism, misranking can only hurt or be unnecessary.
- Given the above, I will submit my true ordering x > z > y > w.

Thus I rank schools in my actual preference order rather than trying to game priorities or others' common preferences.
reasoning.Student B:
I should submit preferences that maximize my chance of getting the best feasible school. Under the usual student-proposing deferred acceptance (DA) mechanism, truthful reporting is a dominant strategy, so I should list my true ranking. Even without that guarantee, given the information about others' rankings (most favor y first) and my priorities, it is strategic to put x first:

- My true top choice is x and I have priority 1 at x, so I am well-positioned to get x if I rank it first.
- I also have priority 1 at z and prefer z to y, while most other applicants rank z last, so z is relatively safe as my second choice.
- Many others favor y first and I have lower priority (2) at y, so ranking y ahead of x or z risks losing those higher-priority applicants for a crowded y; better to place y after x and z.
- w is my least preferred and I have lower priority there, so it belongs last.

Therefore I will submit my true ranking: x > z > y > w.

Under the standard student-proposing deferred-acceptance algorithm — which is strategy-proof for students — it is a weakly dominant strategy to report true preferences, so I should list x first even though my priority at x is low (4) and many applicants favor y.
